reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a groundbreaking theoretical framework for understanding the Chiral Induced Spin Selectivity
(CISS) effect in topological knot molecules. The work is highly original, timely, and scientifically rigorous, offering the first
comprehensive model that accounts for the remarkably high spin polarization, enhanced conductivity, and exceptional
thermal stability observed in recent experimental studies. The introduction of geometric spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as a key
mechanism distinct form conventional SOC in structurally chiral systems is particularly insightful. The multi-terminal device
simulations are well-designed, and the results robustly demonstrate the role of topological chirality and structural asymmetry
in spin-selectivity transport. This study constitutes a significant advance in the field of chiral spintronics and strongly merits
publication in Nature Communications, pending minor revisions as outlined below.
(i) Although the Supplementary Information provides some details on the derivation of Geometric SOC, it would strengthen
the manuscript to include a more explicit derivation or intuitive explanation of the geometric SOC term in the main text or
Methods section.
(ii) The current theoretical value (~60%) shows a discrepancy with the experimental value (~90%), and the author has
attributed this gap to the differences between the single-molecule model and the multilayer structure of the thin film. It is
recommended to supplement the Discussion section with information on the potential contributions of multilayer effects and
many-body interactions (such as electron-electron correlations and electron-phonon coupling) to high polarizability in single
molecules.
(iii) Please ensure consistency in reference formatting, including journal name abbreviations, placement of publication
years, and punctuation. Additionally, double-check all in-text citations for accuracy and correspondence with the reference
list.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper by Sun, et al. establish a theoretical framework to explain the chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) observing
in chiral trefoil knot molecules, thereby propose a new direction “knot-driven spin selectivity” in chiral spintronics. Given that
the chiral knot systems are characterized by topological chirality rather than the structural chirality typically associated with
the traditional CISS effect, the authors propose an alternative theoretical model. This model combines a curvature-driven
geometric spin-orbit coupling (SOC) with a decoherence process to explain why experimental measurements on trefoil knot
molecules report such strong spin polarization alongside high conductance.
As far as I'm concerned, this manuscript has three main highlights, which can be summarized as follows: (i) The observation
of the CISS effect in chiral trefoil knot molecular systems marks a significant experimental breakthrough. However, this effect
originates from topological chirality, unlike the traditional CISS effect which is grounded in the structural chirality of system
like helical chains. This work clearly distinguishes between these two types of chirality and constructs a new theoretical
framework to elucidate the CISS effect induced by topological chirality. (ii) This work introduces a Berry-phase-related
geometric SOC arising from molecular curvature to understand the emergence of spin selectivity and polarization. This
concept is novel and provides valuable insights for future studies on irregular chiral systems. (iii) It reveals for the first time
the evolution of the CISS effect during the phase transition between topological chirality and structural chirality. The
numerical results illustrating this transition process are both compelling and reliable.
Considering the above mentions, I support the publication of this manuscript in Nat. Commun. Below is a list of some
specific concerns that will be useful for the development on this work.
(i) This theoretical study primarily draws upon recent experimental research on the CISS effect in trefoil knot molecules (J.
Am. Chem. Soc. 145, 26791 (2023), e.g., Ref. [66]). As far as I am aware, the experimental work also proposed a theoretical
model to explain the CISS effect in their trefoil-knot molecules (referring to the appendix section of the paper). Why, then, did
the authors establish another theoretical framework to study the CISS in this type of system in this study? I recommend that
the authors address this point in the revised manuscript.
(ii) Given that the geometric spin-orbit coupling (SOC) resulting from the spatial curvature of electron transport serves as the
primary physical mechanism underlying the spin selectivity in this class of chiral materials, it is recommended that the author
provide a detailed discussion and explanation of the main causes and computational methods for generating this type of
SOC, i.e., Geometric SOC, in the "Methods" section of the paper.
(iii) I recommend that the authors modify and improve some statements in the manuscript to enhance the accuracy of the
arguments. For instance, the authors stated, "the ultra-high spin polarization in trefoil knot molecules originates from
topological protection, exhibiting exceptional robustness." However, based on the authors’ computational results, the ultra-
high spin polarization primarily stems from Geometric SOC rather than the topological protection of the topological knot.
Meanwhile, the topological properties of the knot contribute favorably to enhance the stability of the high spin-polarized
states.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors claim to present variation of the chiral induced spin selectivity (CISS) effect, that they call "topological CISS".
Their claim is based on their suggestion that the spin orbit coupling in knot like molecules has three ingredients that they
claim do not all exist in the regular spin orbit coupling considered in the CISS. The three ingredients are the regular "atomic
like" spin orbit coupling (SOC), contribution to the SOC that results from the topology of the system, and the Berry phase that
results in interferences that may enhance the SOC.
Although there is a place to discuss the SOC in knot like molecules because of its size, the "new ingredients" to the SOC do
exist in calculations done in the past also for chiral molecules that are not knots. Actually it is well established that there is a
component that result from the chiral topology that changes sign between the enantiomers. I suggest that the authors will
lokk at the following references:
1. T. P. Fay, Chirality-Induced Spin Coherence in Electron Transfer Reactions, J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 12, 1407-1412 (2021).
2. Fay, T. P.; Limmer, D. T. Origin of chirality induced spin selectivity in photoinduced electron transfer. Nano Lett., 21,
6696−6702 (2021).
3. C. Seibel, J. H. Soh, S. Zilberg, A. I. Krylov, Ultrafast Transversal CISS Effect Observed in a Chiral Photoswitching
Molecule, J. Phys. Chem. Lett., 16, 8514 – 8522 (2025).
Based on the above I suggest a major revision in which the authors will tune down their claims and will suggest their work
as a discussion on the SOC in case of knows.

Response:

substantially expanded the Discussion section (Page 8). We have added a dedicated paragraph that
delves into the potential mechanism that could bridge the gap between our single-molecule prediction
and the experimental thin-film measurements. Specifically, we have enriched the discussion including:
(1) The possibility of constructive spin filtering through a coherent stack of molecular knots in a
multilayer architecture, where the spin polarization could be multiplicatively enhanced.
(2) The potential role of many-body interactions, such as electron-electron corrections leading to
enhanced effective SOC, and electron-phonon coupling potentially influence spin relaxation
dynamics. These factors have contributions to enhance the spin polarization.
Incorporating these structural and many-body effects into future models is expected to bring theoretical
predictions closer to the 90% polarization observed experimentally, thus reconciling the current
discrepancy while affirming the physical consistency of the proposed geometric SOC mechanism. We
may focus on these topics in our future theoretical investigations.

abbreviations, placement of publication years, and punctuation. Additionally, double-check all in-text

of the entire reference list and all in-text citations. The references have been reformatted to ensure strict
compliance with the Nature Communications style, and we have verified the perfect correspondence
between every citation and its entry in the reference list.
Reply to Reviewer #2
We are sincerely grateful to the reviewer for their exceptionally positive and insightful summary of our
work's highlights and for their strong support for publication. Their specific concerns have been
invaluable in further strengthening the narrative and precision of our manuscript.
Comment (i): “This theoretical study primarily draws upon recent experimental research on the CISS
effect in trefoil knot molecules (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 145, 26791 (2023), e.g., Ref. [66]). As far as I am
aware, the experimental work also proposed a theoretical model to explain the CISS effect in their
trefoil-knot molecules (referring to the appendix section of the paper). Why, then, did the authors
establish another theoretical framework to study the CISS in this type of system in this study? I
recommend that the authors address this point in the revised manuscript.”
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. Although the original experimental work
(Ref. [19]) did put forwards a theoretical model and associated methods to explain the observed highly
spin-polarized current, our work has developed a distinct theoretical framework to analyze the CISS
effect in this class of systems. The key considerations behind this approach are summarized as follows:
(1) The original work (Ref. [19]) introduced a qualitative model based on a four-site single helical
chain, a configuration traditionally employed to represent structural chirality, the experimental
system under investigation actually utilized trefoil-knot molecules. These molecules form a closed
topological knot structure, distinct from open chiral chains. As noted by the authors of Ref. [66],
their study addressed topological chirality-induced spin selectivity rather than structural chirality.
Consequently, applying a structural-chirality model to explore topological chirality may be
inadequate for revealing the fundamental physical origins of CISS in such knotted systems. This
limitation constitutes the primary motivation for developing our alternative theoretical framework
focused on topology-induced spin selectivity
(2) We appreciate the reviewer's comment regarding the theoretical treatment of spin-orbit coupling
(SOC). In the original model presented in Ref. [19], SOC is incorporated through a next-nearest
neighbor hopping term within a uniform single helical chain, with the SOC strength parameter λ
taken as a fixed constant (λ = 1 meV). While this approach offers a simplified representation, it
does not account for spatial variations in SOC that arise from the specific geometrical arrangement
of the knot structure. Consequently, such a uniform treatment becomes inadequate for investigating
the influence of structural defects on CISS or for capturing potential phase transitions between
topological and structural chirality, as the local electronic environment in these systems cannot be
properly reflected by a constant SOC value.
(3) In our theoretical framework, we explicitly introduce an inspired geometric spin-orbit coupling
(SOC) that stems from the intrinsic curvature of the entire molecular knot, thereby extending
beyond the conventional SOC formulation rooted solely in structural chirality. A key feature of this
geometric SOC is its direct dependence on the local geometric configuration, being fundamentally
governed by the local curvature of the electron's pathway. Consequently, the strength of this SOC
is not a fixed parameter but varies with the specific geometrical arrangement of the closed knot
molecule. This attribute enables the geometric SOC to more accurately capture the underlying
physics of topological knots, offering a clear advantage over the constant SOC approximation
employed in the original model.
(4) Furthermore, our theoretical model offers a quantitative and microscopic perspective on how
topological chirality and geometric curvature jointly give rise to the observed high spin polarization
and conductance. It also enables self-consistent simulation of nonequilibrium quantum transport in
a multi-terminal device geometry, capturing both bulk and interfacial properties in a unified manner.

highlighted by blue) with the following statement: “… Although pioneering experimental work has
presented a theoretical model to explain the highly spin-polarized current in these systems, the model
itself remains grounded in a simplified picture, that of a uniform helical chain with structural chirality19.
This representation, although valuable, does not fully capture the spatial variations and specific
geometrical arrangement inherent in a knot topology. As a result, it offers limited insight into the
distinctive physical processes that govern CISS in these entangled structures. A dedicated theoretical
framework that directly addresses topological chirality is still needed to clarify the underlying
microscopic mechanisms."

curvature of electron transport serves as the primary physical mechanism underlying the spin
selectivity in this class of chiral materials, it is recommended that the author provide a detailed
discussion and explanation of the main causes and computational methods for generating this type of

polarization in trefoil knot molecules originates from topological protection, exhibiting exceptional
robustness." However, based on the authors’ computational results, the ultra-high spin polarization

phrasing was indeed inaccurate. We have carefully revised the manuscript to reflect this nuanced
understanding. The specific statement has been revised to (see Page 6, the last sentences of the first

precise attribution of the effects to their correct physical origins.

studies by Fay et al. and Seibel et al. to our attention. These feedbacks have been instrumental in
helping us refine the presentation of our results and more precisely situate the novelty and contribution
of our work within the broader context of CISS research.

literature. The reviewer’s insights have helped us to better position our work within the existing field

we discussed, including the contribution from chiral topology and the Berry phase, have indeed been
explored in previous studies of chiral molecules, as exemplified by the references provided.

our work as a detailed investigation into the ‘manifestation and enhancement of the CISS effect

new ingredients. To this end, we have rewritten the third paragraph in the “Introduction”

by offering a detailed and quantitative analysis of SOC in a distinctive group of chiral molecules, i.e.,
molecular knots. Their intricate and well-defined topology enables clearer separation and a potentially
stronger manifestation of effects that are subtler in simpler chiral systems. Moreover, our findings
underscore the potential of molecular knots as a promising platform for observing pronounced CISS-
related phenomena, owing to their marked topological properties.

addresses the reviewer’s concerns and meets with their approval.

### Reviewer 1

This manuscript presents a groundbreaking theoretical framework for understanding the Chiral Induced Spin Selectivity
(CISS) effect in topological knot molecules. The work is highly original, timely, and scientifically rigorous, offering the first
comprehensive model that accounts for the remarkably high spin polarization, enhanced conductivity, and exceptional
thermal stability observed in recent experimental studies. The introduction of geometric spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as a key
mechanism distinct form conventional SOC in structurally chiral systems is particularly insightful. The multi-terminal device
simulations are well-designed, and the results robustly demonstrate the role of topological chirality and structural asymmetry
in spin-selectivity transport. This study constitutes a significant advance in the field of chiral spintronics and strongly merits
publication in Nature Communications, pending minor revisions as outlined below.
(i) Although the Supplementary Information provides some details on the derivation of Geometric SOC, it would strengthen
the manuscript to include a more explicit derivation or intuitive explanation of the geometric SOC term in the main text or
Methods section.
(ii) The current theoretical value (~60%) shows a discrepancy with the experimental value (~90%), and the author has
attributed this gap to the differences between the single-molecule model and the multilayer structure of the thin film. It is
recommended to supplement the Discussion section with information on the potential contributions of multilayer effects and
many-body interactions (such as electron-electron correlations and electron-phonon coupling) to high polarizability in single
molecules.
(iii) Please ensure consistency in reference formatting, including journal name abbreviations, placement of publication
years, and punctuation. Additionally, double-check all in-text citations for accuracy and correspondence with the reference
list.

### Reviewer 2

This paper by Sun, et al. establish a theoretical framework to explain the chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) observing
in chiral trefoil knot molecules, thereby propose a new direction “knot-driven spin selectivity” in chiral spintronics. Given that
the chiral knot systems are characterized by topological chirality rather than the structural chirality typically associated with
the traditional CISS effect, the authors propose an alternative theoretical model. This model combines a curvature-driven
geometric spin-orbit coupling (SOC) with a decoherence process to explain why experimental measurements on trefoil knot
molecules report such strong spin polarization alongside high conductance.
As far as I'm concerned, this manuscript has three main highlights, which can be summarized as follows: (i) The observation
of the CISS effect in chiral trefoil knot molecular systems marks a significant experimental breakthrough. However, this effect
originates from topological chirality, unlike the traditional CISS effect which is grounded in the structural chirality of system
like helical chains. This work clearly distinguishes between these two types of chirality and constructs a new theoretical
framework to elucidate the CISS effect induced by topological chirality. (ii) This work introduces a Berry-phase-related
geometric SOC arising from molecular curvature to understand the emergence of spin selectivity and polarization. This
concept is novel and provides valuable insights for future studies on irregular chiral systems. (iii) It reveals for the first time
the evolution of the CISS effect during the phase transition between topological chirality and structural chirality. The
numerical results illustrating this transition process are both compelling and reliable.
Considering the above mentions, I support the publication of this manuscript in Nat. Commun. Below is a list of some
specific concerns that will be useful for the development on this work.
(i) This theoretical study primarily draws upon recent experimental research on the CISS effect in trefoil knot molecules (J.
Am. Chem. Soc. 145, 26791 (2023), e.g., Ref. [66]). As far as I am aware, the experimental work also proposed a theoretical
model to explain the CISS effect in their trefoil-knot molecules (referring to the appendix section of the paper). Why, then, did
the authors establish another theoretical framework to study the CISS in this type of system in this study? I recommend that
the authors address this point in the revised manuscript.
(ii) Given that the geometric spin-orbit coupling (SOC) resulting from the spatial curvature of electron transport serves as the
primary physical mechanism underlying the spin selectivity in this class of chiral materials, it is recommended that the author
provide a detailed discussion and explanation of the main causes and computational methods for generating this type of
SOC, i.e., Geometric SOC, in the "Methods" section of the paper.
(iii) I recommend that the authors modify and improve some statements in the manuscript to enhance the accuracy of the
arguments. For instance, the authors stated, "the ultra-high spin polarization in trefoil knot molecules originates from
topological protection, exhibiting exceptional robustness." However, based on the authors’ computational results, the ultra-
high spin polarization primarily stems from Geometric SOC rather than the topological protection of the topological knot.
Meanwhile, the topological properties of the knot contribute favorably to enhance the stability of the high spin-polarized
states.

effect in trefoil knot molecules (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 145, 26791 (2023), e.g., Ref. [66]). As far as I am

Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. Although the original experimental work
(Ref. [19]) did put forwards a theoretical model and associated methods to explain the observed highly
spin-polarized current, our work has developed a distinct theoretical framework to analyze the CISS
effect in this class of systems. The key considerations behind this approach are summarized as follows:
(1) The original work (Ref. [19]) introduced a qualitative model based on a four-site single helical
chain, a configuration traditionally employed to represent structural chirality, the experimental
system under investigation actually utilized trefoil-knot molecules. These molecules form a closed
topological knot structure, distinct from open chiral chains. As noted by the authors of Ref. [66],
their study addressed topological chirality-induced spin selectivity rather than structural chirality.
Consequently, applying a structural-chirality model to explore topological chirality may be
inadequate for revealing the fundamental physical origins of CISS in such knotted systems. This
limitation constitutes the primary motivation for developing our alternative theoretical framework
focused on topology-induced spin selectivity
(2) We appreciate the reviewer's comment regarding the theoretical treatment of spin-orbit coupling
(SOC). In the original model presented in Ref. [19], SOC is incorporated through a next-nearest
neighbor hopping term within a uniform single helical chain, with the SOC strength parameter λ
taken as a fixed constant (λ = 1 meV). While this approach offers a simplified representation, it
does not account for spatial variations in SOC that arise from the specific geometrical arrangement
of the knot structure. Consequently, such a uniform treatment becomes inadequate for investigating
the influence of structural defects on CISS or for capturing potential phase transitions between
topological and structural chirality, as the local electronic environment in these systems cannot be
properly reflected by a constant SOC value.
(3) In our theoretical framework, we explicitly introduce an inspired geometric spin-orbit coupling
(SOC) that stems from the intrinsic curvature of the entire molecular knot, thereby extending
beyond the conventional SOC formulation rooted solely in structural chirality. A key feature of this
geometric SOC is its direct dependence on the local geometric configuration, being fundamentally
governed by the local curvature of the electron's pathway. Consequently, the strength of this SOC
is not a fixed parameter but varies with the specific geometrical arrangement of the closed knot
molecule. This attribute enables the geometric SOC to more accurately capture the underlying
physics of topological knots, offering a clear advantage over the constant SOC approximation
employed in the original model.
(4) Furthermore, our theoretical model offers a quantitative and microscopic perspective on how
topological chirality and geometric curvature jointly give rise to the observed high spin polarization
and conductance. It also enables self-consistent simulation of nonequilibrium quantum transport in
a multi-terminal device geometry, capturing both bulk and interfacial properties in a unified manner.
To clarify this important distinction, we have expanded the Introduction (Page 2, Lines 12-19,
highlighted by blue) with the following statement: “… Although pioneering experimental work has
presented a theoretical model to explain the highly spin-polarized current in these systems, the model
itself remains grounded in a simplified picture, that of a uniform helical chain with structural chirality19.
This representation, although valuable, does not fully capture the spatial variations and specific
geometrical arrangement inherent in a knot topology. As a result, it offers limited insight into the
distinctive physical processes that govern CISS in these entangled structures. A dedicated theoretical
framework that directly addresses topological chirality is still needed to clarify the underlying
microscopic mechanisms."
